author: A Robot
objectives: Understand the phenomenon of apparent retrograde motion.
Demonstrate how relative planetary orbital motion creates the illusion of loops.

modules.description: Observation of Mars's apparent retrograde motion in the night sky.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Describe the apparent path of Mars during retrograde motion.
instructions: Watch the red marker representing Mars as it moves across the constellations.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars begins at its starting position in the night sky.
clips.narration: Welcome. Tonight we observe Mars from Earth. Notice it drifting slowly eastward against the stars.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars traces its retrograde loop across the starfield.
clips.narration: Watch closely as Mars slows, reverses into a loop, then continues its eastward drift. Why does it do this?

modules.description: Geocentric explanation using epicycles and deferents.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Contrast geocentric and heliocentric models of planetary motion.
instructions: Observe the orbital machinery. Note how the smaller circle causes the apparent backward motion.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars begins moving on its epicycle path around Earth.
clips.narration: In the geocentric model, Mars moves on an epicycle. When it hits the inner part of this loop, it appears to move backward.

clips.changeMeaning: Add text label to explain the epicycle structure.
clips.narration: While this fits observations, it requires complex, tuned geometry. As data improved, astronomers had to stack more epicycles.

modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why retrograde motion occurs as a consequence of Earth overtaking outer planets.
instructions: Observe Earth's inner, faster orbit as it passes the slower-moving Mars.

clips.changeMeaning: Earth orbits the Sun and overtakes Mars, visually representing the heliocentric explanation.
clips.narration: From the heliocentric view, the loop vanishes. Earth simply overtakes the slower Mars. No epicycles needed.
